kp.k: Unverified AI drafting resulted in monetary attorney sanctions
kp.d: The Fifth Circuit found that Heather Hersh used generative AI to draft a substantial portion, potentially all, of her appellate reply brief without checking its accuracy. Its show-cause order identified 16 instances of fabricated quotations and 5 additional serious misrepresentations of law or fact. The February 18, 2026 opinion imposed a $2,500 sanction payable within 30 days, based on both the unchecked filing and counsel’s subsequent lack of candor. This sanction was distinct from the underlying district-court sanctions against Shawn Jaffer and his firm, which the appellate court had vacated.
qs: We issued a show-cause order, enumerating 16 instances of fabricated quotations and 5 additional serious misrepresentations of law or fact.
In sum, the court finds that Hersh used artificial generative intelligence to draft a substantial portion—if not all—of her reply brief and failed to check the brief for accuracy.
IT IS ORDERED that Heather Hersh shall pay $2,500 in sanctions to the United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit within 30 days of this order.

kp.k: Existing disciplinary powers govern AI-related professional misconduct
kp.d: The court maintained that AI does not require a separate sanctions framework. It relied on Federal Rule of Appellate Procedure 46(c), which permits attorney discipline including monetary sanctions, and its inherent power to sanction abuse of the judicial process. It treated unchecked misrepresentations of law and misleading explanations as misconduct under these existing powers, also citing Texas professional-conduct rules concerning frivolous assertions, false statements and dishonesty.
qs: Modern generative AI may be a new technology, but the same sanctions rules apply, and the rules we have are well equipped to handle these types of cases.
Discipline under Rule 46(c) may include monetary sanctions.
Hersh’s misleading the court as to the source of her errors further justifies sanctions under our inherent powers.

kp.k: The circuit rejected a separate AI certification requirement
kp.d: The opinion recounts a proposed rule requiring counsel and self-represented litigants to certify either that no generative AI had been used or that a human had checked generated text for accuracy. Thirteen comments came from judges, professors and practitioners; many argued that existing accuracy obligations made the rule unnecessary. Following its AI Subcommittee’s recommendation, the court declined adoption and instead issued a reminder to review all filings for accuracy.
qs: Thirteen comments were submitted by judges, professors, and practitioners.
Ultimately, the Subcommittee recommended to the court that we decline to adopt the proposed rule, and we followed the Subcommittee’s recommendation.
In doing so, we concluded that existing rules were sufficient to deter misconduct related to generative AI use, without the need for a rule specific to generative AI.

kp.k: Ethical AI assistance requires human verification of legal authority
kp.d: The court expressly accepted that carefully used generative AI can assist legal practice, but rejected ignorance of its risks as an excuse for submitting unchecked work. Quoting ByoPlanet, it required lawyers to ensure generated legal propositions and authorities are trustworthy. The obligation concerns substantive accuracy, rather than simply acknowledging AI use; counsel’s failure to explain any verification steps contributed to the court’s conclusion that none had been taken.
qs: If it were ever an excuse to plead ignorance of the risks of using generative AI to draft a brief without verifying its output, it is certainly no longer so.

To ethically use generative AI in the practice of law—which we do not dispute can be helpful if done properly and carefully—a lawyer must “ensure that the legal propositions and authority generated are trustworthy.”
Even when asked directly, Hersh did not explain the steps she took to verify the factual assertions in her brief, so the court concludes that she took none.

kp.k: Fabricated quotations in real cases complicate error detection
kp.d: The opinion contrasts the nonexistent cases in Mata v. Avianca with false quotations or legal propositions attributed to genuine authorities. Citing OpenAI on training and model structures and Jane Bambauer on increasingly persuasive fabrications, the court argues that hallucinations remain persistent and harder to detect as models become more sophisticated. These are the opinion’s broader claims supported by cited commentary, not measured model-performance findings from this proceeding.
qs: The hallucination problem has no end in sight, as AI’s tendency to fabricate results arises from the training and structures of AI programs.
As time goes on, these hallucinations grow “all the more insidious and harder to guard against,” as the models are more sophisticated and appear more truthful.
This problem now often manifests as false quotes or statements of law attributed to real cases, rather than the more easily recognizable fake cases.

kp.k: Reported hallucination incidents burden courts despite repeated warnings
kp.d: Citing Damien Charlotin’s database of court orders, the opinion reports 239 United States cases of hallucination by lawyers as of February 18, 2026, excluding hallucinations introduced by self-represented litigants and judges. It characterizes the problem as worsening despite public reporting, continuing legal education, scholarship and judicial warnings, and lists district-court incidents within the circuit. The count concerns court incidents, not a model error rate or the prevalence of hallucinations across all filings.
qs: As of the date of this order, Charlotin has identified 239 cases of hallucination by lawyers in the United States.
This figure excludes hallucinations introduced by pro se litigants and judges.
It is a problem that is getting worse—not better.

kp.k: Source explanations failed scrutiny and consumed judicial resources
kp.d: Hersh initially attributed errors to publicly available cases and paraphrased summaries, later identifying Google Scholar, CourtListener, Justia, FindLaw, Casetext and vLex. The court said it could not locate the disputed language in the non-AI sources it reviewed and characterized the remaining two sources as generative AI products. It did not establish which product generated the errors; its criticism of those possible sources was conditional. It also rejected the claim that AI had merely organized arguments and shortened paragraphs, and emphasized the effort expended investigating the alleged summaries.
qs: The court does not find it credible that these sources produced the hallucinated quotations that appeared in Hersh’s brief.
We do not find it credible that Hersh used AI solely to “help organize and structure [her] arguments and to break up overly long paragraphs.”
We have put tremendous effort into attempting to find where these summaries could be located and have been unable to find them.

kp.k: Candor after discovery materially affects sanctions
kp.d: The court found Hersh’s explanations evasive and misleading, noting that she omitted AI from her initial response and admitted use only when specifically questioned. It stated that greater candor and acceptance of responsibility likely would have reduced the sanction. Separately, it described AI use in her show-cause response as likely, rather than an established finding. The opinion also noted a previous federal-court sanction and emphasized that any earlier discovery of errors should have prompted immediate notification and a request to correct the brief.
qs: Further, Hersh did not even mention AI in her first response to the court.
It is also likely that she used artificial generative intelligence in her response to the show-cause order.
Had Hersh accepted responsibility and been more forthcoming, it is likely that the court would have imposed lesser sanctions.
However, when confronted with a serious ethical misstep, Hersh misled, evaded, and violated her duties as an officer of this court.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The court claims that AI-generated fabrications in legal filings are worsening and becoming harder to detect; useful legal AI use requires human verification, while existing disciplinary rules remain applicable.
pts.d: Chief Judge Elrod, writing for the Fifth Circuit, states that hallucinations arise from AI training and structure and have no foreseeable end. The opinion describes an increasingly difficult detection problem: false quotations and legal propositions attributed to actual cases rather than wholly invented cases. It acknowledges that generative AI can help legal practice when used carefully, but places responsibility for accuracy on lawyers. The court concludes that existing sanctions powers can address AI-related misconduct without a technology-specific rule. In this case, it finds that Heather Hersh used AI to draft a substantial portion, if not all, of her reply brief without checking accuracy and then responded evasively. The $2,500 sanction addresses both the unverified filing and lack of candor, not AI use alone.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The opinion relies on its examination of the filing and counsel’s responses, other sanctions cases, a database of court incidents, and cited technical and scholarly commentary.
pts.d: The court enumerates 16 fabricated quotations and five additional serious misrepresentations in Hersh’s brief. It reports checking the named legal databases and finding no support for the disputed quotations and propositions; it infers lack of verification from counsel’s failure to explain any checking steps. Its broader claim about growing problems draws on Mata v. Avianca, subsequent sanctions decisions, and Damien Charlotin’s database, which it reports contained 239 U.S. lawyer hallucination cases as of February 18, 2026, excluding incidents involving pro se litigants and judges. This is an incident count, not a measured model error rate or a benchmark; the opinion does not provide a comparable time series to quantify growth. It cites OpenAI on why models hallucinate and Jane Bambauer on increasingly difficult detection. Its claim about the sufficiency of existing rules rests on the court’s rulemaking experience, Federal Rule of Appellate Procedure 46(c), inherent judicial powers, and sanctions precedents. It does not establish which particular AI product generated the errors.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The opinion describes an ongoing problem as of February 18, 2026, predicts no identifiable end, and conditions acceptable AI use on careful verification.
pts.d: The court situates the problem between the high-profile Mata incident in 2023 and the date of this opinion, February 18, 2026. Its forward-looking statements are qualitative rather than tied to a deadline or quantified forecast. It says ignorance of unverified AI drafting risks is no longer an excuse. The qualification that AI can be helpful when used properly distinguishes supervised assistance from reliance on unchecked output. Counsel who discovers errors after filing should immediately notify the court and seek permission to correct the brief. The actual sanction must be paid within 30 days; the court also indicates that greater candor and acceptance of responsibility likely would have reduced the sanction.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: Lawyers retain responsibility and face discipline; courts and adversaries bear the burden of false filings, and professional credibility is at risk.
pts.d: The immediate affected lawyer is Hersh, the sole signatory of the reply brief, whom the court orders to pay $2,500. More broadly, practicing lawyers must verify AI-generated legal propositions, citations, quotations, and factual assertions before relying on them. Courts incur work investigating errors and addressing misleading explanations; the opinion describes substantial effort searching for counsel’s alleged source summaries. Adversaries can incur costs responding to fabricated citations, including those submitted by pro se litigants, whom the court says are not immune from sanctions. The court endorses the concern that failure to verify wastes legal resources and undermines public respect for the profession and judicial proceedings. It makes no concrete prediction about legal employment, firm staffing, pricing, or market shares.
